client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed with anxiety about my final exams coming up next month. After struggling with my coursework last term, it’s hard to shake the feeling that I won't be able to handle it this time either. Sometimes, I wonder if therapy can really help me with this kind of pressure.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden with the anxiety surrounding your final exams, especially after the challenges you faced last term. I can sense that there's a lot of pressure you're feeling, and it's completely valid to question how therapy can support you in this situation. What do you think is making it hard for you to believe in your ability to handle the pressure this time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think a lot of it comes from my past experiences. Last term, I felt like I was constantly falling behind and never really caught up, which made me doubt my abilities. I just can’t shake the feeling that if I struggled before, what’s to say I won’t struggle again? It’s hard to trust that I can change things this time around.
therapist: It sounds like your past experiences are really weighing on you and influencing how you feel about your capabilities now. I can hear that sense of doubt when you talk about trusting yourself to handle things this time. What specific changes or support do you think would help you feel more confident as you approach your exams?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think I would feel more confident if I had a clear study plan and maybe some accountability, like checking in with a friend or study group. But then I worry that even with a plan, I might not stick to it or that I'll get too anxious to focus when I try to study. It just feels like there's so much uncertainty, and I'm not sure if a plan would really make a difference for me.
therapist: It seems like you have some solid ideas about what could help you feel more confident, like having a study plan and accountability. Yet, I can hear that uncertainty creeping in about whether those strategies would really work for you. What do you think might be holding you back from fully embracing the idea of a plan, even if it feels like it could provide some structure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess part of me worries that if I try to stick to a plan and then fail, it’ll just confirm my fears about not being good enough. There's this voice in my head that says I’ll let myself down again, and that’s really paralyzing. I want to believe that a plan could help, but I’m scared it might just add more pressure instead of relieving it.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really torn between wanting to create a plan and the fear of it not working out, which is understandably paralyzing. That inner voice can be powerful and discouraging, making it hard to move forward. What do you think could help you challenge that voice and create a more supportive mindset as you consider making a plan?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I’m not really sure how to challenge that voice. It feels so ingrained, like a part of me that I can't just shut off. I guess I could try to remind myself of times when I did succeed or at least made progress, but even that feels like a stretch right now. What if I can’t think of anything positive?
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling stuck with that negative voice, making it difficult to see any moments of success or progress. I can sense the struggle you're experiencing, and it's okay to feel that way. What if we took a moment to explore even small instances where you felt a sense of achievement or growth, no matter how minor they might seem? Sometimes, even the tiniest victories can help shift our perspective.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I suppose there have been a few moments where I felt like I accomplished something, like when I managed to finish a project on time, even if it was a struggle. But those moments feel overshadowed by the times I didn’t do well, and I worry that they don't really count. It’s hard to focus on those small victories when my mind keeps replaying the failures. It makes me wonder if looking back at those moments will really help me feel more confident now.
therapist: It’s encouraging to hear you acknowledge those moments of accomplishment, even if they feel overshadowed by your struggles. I can sense the frustration in your voice when you talk about replaying those failures, which can make it hard to appreciate your successes. What if we took some time to explore what those achievements meant to you, even if they feel small? It might help to see how they connect to your ability to move forward.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess I can see how those small achievements might mean something, like finishing that project showed me I can push through when things get tough. But even acknowledging that feels risky because I don't want to get my hopes up. What if I try to focus on those moments and still end up feeling disappointed again? It just feels like a lot to put myself out there again.
therapist: It's great to hear you recognize the significance of those small achievements, like pushing through with your project. I can sense the hesitance you're feeling about fully embracing that acknowledgment, as it feels risky to hope for more. It’s completely understandable to worry about disappointment, especially after past experiences. What if we explored ways to celebrate those small wins without putting too much pressure on yourself? How might that look for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of celebrating those small wins, but I’m not sure how to do that without feeling silly or like I’m just trying to convince myself everything is okay. Maybe I could write them down, but I worry that it won't feel genuine if I'm just forcing myself to do it. It feels tough to find a balance between recognizing my efforts and not putting too much pressure on myself to feel good about them.
therapist: It's wonderful that you're open to the idea of celebrating your small wins, even though it feels tricky to find the right approach. I can hear that you're worried about coming off as insincere, which is a valid concern. What if you approached it in a way that feels authentic to you? Perhaps by jotting down your achievements without any pressure to feel a certain way about them, just allowing yourself to acknowledge those moments as they come. How does that sound to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think writing down my achievements without any pressure could be a good start, but I still feel skeptical about whether it will really help. It seems like it could turn into just another task I have to do, and I might end up feeling even more anxious if I can’t think of anything to write. I guess I’m just worried that this won't actually change how I feel about my abilities.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling a bit skeptical about the idea of writing down your achievements, as you’re worried it might turn into just another task that adds to your anxiety. I appreciate your honesty about that concern. What if we thought about a more flexible approach, where you only write down achievements when they naturally come to mind, without any pressure? How might that feel for you as a way to acknowledge your efforts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That sounds a bit better, actually. If I only write things down when they come to mind, it feels less daunting and more natural. But I still worry that I might not remember to do it or that it won’t make a difference in how I feel about my abilities. What if I end up forgetting about it altogether?
therapist: I'm glad to hear that the more flexible approach feels better for you! It’s understandable to worry about remembering to write things down and whether it will truly impact how you feel about your abilities. That uncertainty can be overwhelming. What if you considered setting a gentle reminder for yourself, or even finding a way to make it a part of your routine, like a quick reflection at the end of each day? How does that idea sit with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
